subtopics.title: Why Nations Trade — Absolute and Comparative Advantage

questions.question: A country has an ABSOLUTE advantage in a good when:
options: It can produce the good with fewer resources than another country — more output per worker
It gives up the least of other goods to produce it
It has the largest population
It exports more than it imports

questions.question: Comparative advantage says a country should specialise where:
options: Its workers are most numerous
Its opportunity cost is lowest — where it gives up least by producing that good rather than another
Its absolute advantage is largest in every good
Its currency is strongest

questions.question: With the same resources, South Africa can make 100 maize or 50 steel; Germany 120 maize or 240 steel. A ton of steel costs each country, in maize:
options: South Africa half a ton, Germany two tons
Both exactly one ton
South Africa two tons, Germany half a ton — so Germany should specialise in steel and South Africa in maize
South Africa nothing, Germany nothing

questions.question: The deepest result of comparative advantage is that:
options: Only the most efficient country gains from trade
Trade is zero-sum: one side's gain is the other's loss
Countries with no absolute advantage cannot trade
Both countries can consume beyond their own production possibilities even when one is absolutely better at everything

questions.question: A foreign tourist's spending in Cape Town is recorded as:
options: A service export on the current account
A merchandise import
Portfolio investment on the financial account
A change in official reserves

questions.question: Portfolio investment is nicknamed "hot money" because:
options: It earns the highest interest
Purchases of shares and bonds can be reversed and withdrawn quickly
It is always invested in energy
It is illegal under exchange control

questions.question: A current-account deficit must be matched by:
options: An equal current-account surplus the next year
A trade surplus
A financial-account surplus — foreigners acquiring our assets to finance our net imports — or a fall in reserves
Devaluation of the currency

questions.question: The IMF's loans are controversial because:
options: They are interest-free
They are only given to wealthy countries
The IMF has no member countries
They arrive tied to conditions — typically spending cuts, tax reform and liberalisation

subtopics.title: The Foreign Exchange Market and How the Rand Is Priced

questions.question: On the foreign exchange diagram for dollars, the axes are:
options: Quantity of dollars on the horizontal axis and the rand price of a dollar on the vertical
Time on the horizontal and GDP on the vertical
Rand quantity on the vertical and dollar price on the horizontal
Exports on both axes

questions.question: The SUPPLY of dollars to the South African market comes from:
options: Importers of oil and electronics
Foreigners buying our coal and wine, tourists arriving here, and foreign investors buying our bonds and factories
South Africans travelling abroad
Firms repaying dollar loans

questions.question: The oil price doubles. On the diagram:
options: The supply of dollars shifts right and the rand appreciates
Nothing changes because oil is priced in rands
The demand for dollars shifts right, the rand price of a dollar rises, and the rand depreciates
The demand for dollars shifts left

questions.question: DEVALUATION differs from DEPRECIATION in that devaluation is:
options: Any fall in the currency's value
A market movement under floating rates
An increase in the currency's value
A deliberate downward change made by a government under a fixed exchange rate

questions.question: Under a floating rate, a balance-of-payments deficit tends to self-correct because:
options: Excess demand for foreign currency depreciates the rand, making exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home
The IMF automatically pays the difference
Reserves rise automatically
Import demand always doubles

questions.question: The cost of correcting a deficit through contractionary demand management is:
options: Runaway inflation
Slower growth and higher unemployment — the deficit is cured by making the patient poorer
A larger budget surplus
Automatic appreciation

questions.question: Direct controls such as tariffs, quotas and exchange control carry the risk of:
options: Excessive foreign investment
Too much competition among importers
Retaliation by trading partners, evasion, and the inefficiencies of a rationed market — within limits set by WTO rules
Immediate currency appreciation

questions.question: A persistent SURPLUS is corrected by:
options: Depreciating the currency further
Raising tariffs on imports
Cutting all government spending
Running the toolkit in reverse — allowing appreciation, expanding domestic demand and liberalising imports

questions.question: Sipho bakes for both households and Anna raises the chickens because:
options: Each doing what wastes least effort leaves both eating better than either could alone
A law requires them to specialise
Anna cannot bake at all
Sipho refuses to eat chicken

questions.question: Even when Anna is better at BOTH baking and farming, she still gains by trading with Sipho because:
options: Sipho pays her extra
An hour of baking costs Anna two chickens but costs Sipho almost nothing — her baking hour is expensive to her, so she should pour it into the chicken run
Her ovens are broken
Charity requires it

questions.question: "Countries are Sipho and Anna with flags" means:
options: Countries never specialise
Only neighbouring countries trade
Nations, like the neighbours, gain by doing what costs them least and trading for the rest
Trade requires a formal treaty first

questions.question: The catch at the fence — Anna will not take bread coupons forever — points to:
options: The failure of comparative advantage
The need for tariffs
Anna's absolute advantage
The question of whose money settles the deal — the foreign exchange problem

subtopics.title: The Rand Has a Price Tag Too

questions.question: The queue BUYING dollars with rands contains:
options: The fuel importer, the phone importer, the family paying overseas fees and the fund buying American shares
The coal exporter and the wine estate
German tourists at the waterfront
Foreign funds buying our bonds

questions.question: A long queue at the buy-dollars window and a short queue at the sell window means:
options: The rand appreciates
The dollar gets dearer and the rand weakens — depreciation
The exchange rate cannot move
The Reserve Bank must print dollars

questions.question: "Foreign funds fall in love with our bonds" moves the rand by:
options: Lengthening the buy-dollar queue and weakening the rand
Having no effect on the market
Bringing dollars to the sell window, so the rand firms — appreciation
Forcing devaluation

questions.question: "Floating is bumpy but honest; fixed is calm until it snaps" summarises:
options: Why South Africa fixes the rand to the dollar
The IMF's lending rules
The difference between demand and supply
Floating rates absorb shocks with volatility, while fixed rates give calm certainty until speculators bet the defence must break

subtopics.title: When the Family Spends More Than It Earns

questions.question: In the family notebook, the earning and spending columns, the covering column, and the tin on the shelf correspond to:
options: The current account, the financial account, and the official reserves
GDP, GNI and the deflator
The budget, the deficit and the Laffer curve
Exports, imports and the multiplier

questions.question: The uncle who starts adding conditions to his loans stands for:
options: The World Trade Organisation
The IMF — the lender approached when nobody else will cover the gap, whose conditions are as unwelcome nationally as at the kitchen table
The Reserve Bank
A commercial bank overdraft

questions.question: The depreciating rand is the family's labour getting cheaper to the world, which corrects the gap by:
options: Raising the price of exports abroad
Ending all imports immediately
Making our goods a bargain abroad and imports dear at home, so export volumes rise and import volumes shrink
Increasing the import bill

questions.question: Matching the cure to the disease means:
options: Always borrowing first
Using all four corrections at once in every case
Never using direct controls under any circumstances
A family that overspends needs the belt — demand restraint — while one whose labour is overpriced needs the price cut — depreciation
